title: A starry night in another galaxy
caption: Stars at the center of the Large Magellanic Cloud, imaged in infrared by ESO’s VISTA telescope
celestial: Large Magellanic Cloud, center · constellations Dorado and Mensa

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week, September 2026 (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Millions of stars crowd this infrared view, and almost none of them belong to the Milky Way. ESO’s VISTA telescope zoomed into the center of the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of our neighboring galaxies, to show a starry night from another galaxy.

Galactic centers are hard to observe: dust partly hides them, and their stars are packed so tightly that they blur together. VISTA’s high-resolution infrared camera sees through much of the dust. Over several years, a team led by Maria-Rosa Cioni of the Leibniz Institute for Astrophysics in Potsdam observed the cores of the Magellanic Clouds about 40 times.

All those visits let the team measure the tiny motions of the stars, which is key to finding the exact center of each galaxy. By following stars whose brightness changes regularly, a way to gauge distance, astronomers hope to rebuild the three-dimensional shape of these galactic cores.

understand.summary: ESO's VISTA telescope, in near-infrared light. The release doesn't publish the filters or color mapping.
understand.eye: This is near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, so the colors are assigned. To the eye, the Large Magellanic Cloud looks like a faint, detached patch of the Milky Way.

behind.people: See full credit: ESO/M.-R. Cioni et al.
behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The data are now public, so other astronomers can explore them too. Most of the Large Magellanic Cloud’s light comes from stars like these, too far away to see one by one without a large telescope. The sky position here is the Large Magellanic Cloud’s center, from standard catalogs; the release gives none.
alt: A dense field of countless stars of many colors, with patches of faint dusty glow.
